fact: Chicago Crime Commission’s 2013 Public Enemy No. 1 page says the Commission “officially joined forces with the DEA Chicago Field Division in 2013 when we put the spotlight on Joaquín Guzmán Loera, aka ‘El Chapo’ by dignifying him as Chicago’s Public Enemy Number One,” and says he was arrested in Mazatlán, Sinaloa, on February 22, 2014.

On February 14, 2013, the Chicago Crime Commission announced at a Chicago news conference that Joaquín Guzmán Loera was its “Public Enemy Number One,” using the exact label “Chicago’s Public Enemy Number One.”
A Chicago federal indictment described Guzmán’s organization as using Chicago “as a distribution hub” and sought forfeiture of “more than $1.8 billion in cash proceeds.”

Judge Brian M. Cogan sentenced Joaquín Archivaldo Guzmán Loera on July 17, 2019, to life imprisonment plus 30 years and ordered $12.6 billion in forfeiture, which was the amount prosecutors said represented drug proceeds traceable to the conspiracy.

Between 1990 and December 2008, the Chicago and Brooklyn indictments said Guzman-Loera and others were responsible for importing nearly 200 metric tons of cocaine and smuggling more than $5.8 billion in cash proceeds.
A Chicago federal complaint alleged that more than $100 million in narcotics proceeds were laundered through Chicago-area defendants and entities.

A 2009 DEA release said Chicago indictments alleged the organization was responsible for importing nearly 200 metric tons of cocaine and smuggling more than $5.8 billion in cash proceeds from narcotics sales back to Mexico.
The same 2009 DEA release said the indictments collectively sought forfeiture of more than $5.8 billion in drug proceeds.

The available primary sources establish forfeiture claims exceeding $5.8 billion in drug proceeds and a separate Chicago laundering case alleging more than $100 million, but do not provide a complete traced end-to-end asset map in the cited filings.
The court ordered Guzman Loera to pay $12.6 billion in forfeiture.
Narcotics seizures totaled over 130,000 kilograms of cocaine and heroin.
Weapons seized included AK-47s and a rocket-propelled grenade launcher.
More than $400,000 worth of assorted jewelry, several luxury automobiles and smaller amounts of cash and electronics equipment were seized and forfeited in administrative proceedings by the DEA.
In late 2008, the Flores brothers' cooperation also facilitated seizures of more than $15 million in cash in the Chicago area.
In late 2008, the Flores brothers' cooperation facilitated the seizure of more than 1,600 kilograms of cocaine in the Los Angeles area that was bound for Chicago.
The eighth superseding indictment seeks forfeiture of $2 billion.
Anguiano Hernandez's indictment seeks forfeiture of $950,000.
Torres's indictment seeks forfeiture of $1 million.
Covarrubias's indictment seeks forfeiture of $2.89 million.

Money laundering conspiracy charges against Anguiano Hernandez, Torres and Covarrubias carry a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison, a $500,000 fine, or an alternate fine totaling twice the amount of funds involved in illegal activity.
Narcotics importation and distribution conspiracy charges carry a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years to a maximum of life in prison and a $10 million fine.
The Chicago-based investigation of the Sinaloa Cartel has resulted in total seizures of approximately $30.8 million since 2008.
The Chicago-based investigation has resulted in seizures of approximately 11 tons of cocaine since 2008.
The Chicago-based investigation has resulted in seizures of 265 kilograms of methamphetamine since 2008.
The Chicago-based investigation has resulted in seizures of 78 kilograms of heroin since 2008.

DEA and contemporaneous reporting consistently described Guzmán as about 5 feet 6 inches tall with a slight build, and the nickname “El Chapo” means “shorty” in Spanish, a moniker widely reported as coming from his stature rather than from Guzmán himself.

In Chicago, federal law enforcement unsealed an eighth superseding indictment on January 27, 2015 that charged nine defendants, including Joaquín Guzmán Loera, and alleged a conspiracy running from May 2005 through December 2014 to import and distribute narcotics and launder money.

DEA Chicago Division Special Agent in Charge Robert J. Bell and Northern District of Illinois U.S. Attorney John R. Lausch, Jr. publicly announced the March 12, 2021 Chicago indictment of five alleged Sinaloa Cartel associates.

Public reporting says Ismael Zambada-Niebla pleaded guilty and was cooperating with Chicago prosecutors, but the details of his cooperation and the full investigative record remained largely undisclosed in public accounts.

The Chicago case overlapped with broader federal cartel prosecutions: DEA said the 2009 Brooklyn and Chicago indictments together charged Guzmán Loera, Ismael Zambada-García, Arturo Beltrán-Leyva, and others with importing nearly 200 metric tons of cocaine into the United States.
The Chicago case unsealed in 2009 charged a large distribution cell in Chicago of which 16 individuals were charged in the indictment.

Beginning no later than in or about May 2008 and continuing until at least on or about April 5, 2023, the Chicago-centered Sinaloa Cartel conspiracy named Joaquín Guzmán Loera as a co-leader and alleged operations in the Northern District of Illinois, Eastern Division, and elsewhere.
The Northern District of Illinois indictment and related releases name Joaquín Guzmán Loera, Ismael Zambada-García, and the Sinaloa Cartel as the core criminal enterprise.
On February 12, 2019, Guzmán Loera was convicted by a federal jury on all 10 counts of the superseding indictment, including narcotics trafficking, firearm offenses, and money laundering conspiracy.
The DEA said the case was investigated by the DEA, ICE HSI, and the FBI, in cooperation with Mexican, Ecuadorian, Netherlands, Dominican, and Colombian law enforcement authorities.
The Chicago money-laundering complaint identified Pineda-Sanchez, Parra-Pedroza, Jose Abel Mendoza-Parra, Maria Loera-Alvarado, and Ernesto Ruiz-Ramirez as defendants in a laundering conspiracy.
The Northern District of Illinois filing states the charged conduct included violations of 21 U.S.C. §§ 841, 846, and 963, and 18 U.S.C. § 1956(h).

DEA and federal prosecutors linked the Chicago case to a long-running transnational drug-trafficking enterprise operating from at least 2008 through 2023, showing how the organization used Chicago as a U.S. distribution and laundering hub.

The 2009 DEA release said Chicago indictments collectively targeted a network responsible for massive cocaine imports and the bulk smuggling of billions in proceeds, underscoring why Chicago was viewed as a major cartel hub.
Joaquin Archivaldo Guzman Loera was sentenced by U.S. District Judge Brian M. Cogan.
Guzman Loera received a life term of imprisonment plus 30 years, with the 30 years running consecutive to the life sentence.
The life sentence was for being a principal leader of a continuing criminal enterprise.
The continuing criminal enterprise charge includes 26 drug-related violations and one murder conspiracy.
Guzman Loera was convicted by a federal jury on February 12, 2019.
The trial lasted three months.
Guzman Loera was convicted on all 10 counts of the superseding indictment.
The 10 counts included narcotics trafficking, using a firearm in furtherance of drug crimes, and participating in a money laundering conspiracy.
The sentence was announced on July 17, 2019.
Guzman Loera is known by aliases including 'El Chapo' and 'El Rapido.'
The Sinaloa Cartel is described as a Mexico-based international drug trafficking organization.
The Sinaloa Cartel was responsible for importing and distributing more than one million kilograms of cocaine, marijuana, methamphetamine, and heroin in the United States.

Guzman Loera maintained control through a sophisticated communications network.
